title: count, for_each, and the meta-arguments that shape a resource

videos.script: The shop needs three subnets that differ in one line. Copying the block three times works, until there are twelve. {{copies}} Terraform has a better answer. One resource block, and a single argument that asks for as many copies as you need. {{count}} The catch is how each copy is named. With count, a copy is a number. Ana removes the middle subnet, and the plan wants to destroy two of them. {{shift}} Nothing is broken. The numbers moved, and Terraform matches on numbers. With for_each, each copy has a name you chose, and the same removal touches only one. {{keys}} Then the real network, already built with numbers, has to change to names. A moved block tells Terraform where each subnet went, and the plan creates nothing and destroys nothing. {{moved}} Two more tools finish the lesson. Dynamic blocks repeat what sits inside a resource. A provider alias sends one bucket to another region. {{alias}} By the end you will know which to reach for, and how to read a plan before it costs you a subnet. {{choose}}
